36.0.big: Populations grow, shrink and interact with other species, and animal behavior is shaped by natural selection too.
points: This chapter is the core of AP ecology: population growth, life strategies, human population, community interactions, and behavioral biology.

36.1.big: Demography is the statistics of populations: how many, how crowded, how spread out, and who's dying when.
points: Population size (N) = how many. Population density = how many per area (size ÷ area).

Counting: a quadrat (count everything in sample squares; good for plants and slow animals) or mark and recapture (mark some, release, recapture later; N = marked × total recaptured ÷ marked recaptured). Animals that learn to avoid traps cause an overestimate; ones that seek out bait cause an underestimate.
Species dispersion pattern: random, uniform (evenly spaced, often from competition or chemicals that keep neighbors away), or clumped (most common: around resources or in herds).
A life table tracks the mortality rate and life expectancy by age. A demographic-based population model uses birth and death rates to predict changes.
Survivorship curve: Type I (most live long and die old: humans, elephants), Type II (steady death rate at all ages: some birds, turtles), Type III (most die young: fish, frogs, salmon).

36.2.big: A species' life history is how it spends its energy budget: lots of cheap offspring, or a few well cared for.
points: Fecundity = how many offspring an individual can produce. High fecundity usually means little parental care.
Semelparity = reproduce once, then die (salmon, many insects). Iteroparity = reproduce many times (most mammals, birds).
Every organism has a limited energy budget to split between growth, survival and reproduction. Late breeders (albatrosses) risk dying before ever reproducing.

36.3.big: With unlimited resources, populations grow exponentially (a J-curve). In the real world they level off at the carrying capacity (an S-curve).
points: Birth rate (B) − death rate (D) = the population growth rate. Biotic potential (rmax) = the fastest possible growth rate: high for fleas and bacteria, low for elephants.
Exponential growth: dN/dt = rmax·N, a J-shaped growth curve. It happens with plenty of resources (bacteria in fresh medium, a species arriving somewhere new).

Logistic growth: dN/dt = rmax·N·(K − N)/K, an S-shaped growth curve. Growth slows as N approaches the carrying capacity (K), the most the environment can support. K can change (drought, new food, disease).
36.3.tip: J = no limits. S = slows down and flattens at K.

36.4.big: Things that limit populations either depend on how crowded it is or don't.
points: Density-dependent regulation: effects get stronger as the population gets crowded: competition (intraspecific competition within the species), disease, predation, waste buildup.
Density-independent regulation: hits no matter the density: fires, floods, freezes, pesticides, weather.
r-selected species: many small offspring, little care, mature fast, short life (insects, frogs, weeds). Favored in unstable environments.
K-selected species: few large offspring, lots of care, mature slowly, long life (elephants, whales, humans). Favored in stable, crowded environments.
Modern view: the r/K idea is a simplification. Real species mix traits shaped by their environment.

36.5.big: Humans have grown exponentially by repeatedly raising their own carrying capacity through agriculture, medicine and technology.
points: Tools, language, farming, domesticated animals, sanitation, vaccines, and fossil-fuel machinery all raised K. Overusing resources can lower it.
Age structure diagrams: a wide base (many young people) = rapid growth, typical of less-developed countries. Column-like = slow or stable growth. Narrow base = shrinking (Japan, parts of Europe).
Zero population growth = births equal deaths. China's one-child policy was an attempt to slow growth.
Consequences: habitat loss, pollution, climate change, biodiversity loss, more CO₂. Humanity's ecological footprint already exceeds one Earth.

36.6.big: Species in a community interact through predation, competition and symbiosis, and communities change over time through succession.
points: Predator-prey cycles: prey rise → predators rise → prey fall → predators fall (the predator peak lags behind the prey peak).

Defenses: camouflage; aposematic coloration (bright warning colors); Batesian mimicry (a harmless species looks like a dangerous one); Müllerian mimicry (two harmful species look alike); Emsleyan/Mertensian mimicry (a deadly species looks like a less harmful one).
Interspecific competition between species: the competitive exclusion principle says two species can't share exactly the same resources forever. One wins, or they divide the resources.
Symbiosis: mutualism (both benefit: bees and flowers), commensalism (one benefits, the other unaffected), parasitism (a parasite benefits and its host is harmed).
Community traits: species richness (number of species), relative species abundance (how common each is). Island biogeography: big islands close to the mainland hold more species.

Foundation species build the habitat (coral). A keystone species has an outsized effect, and the community collapses without it (sea otters, prairie dogs). Invasive species spread without natural controls.

After an environmental disturbance: primary succession starts on bare rock with pioneer species (lichens). Secondary succession follows a fire or flood where soil remains. Both move toward a stable climax community.

36.7.big: Ethology studies animal behavior: what triggers it (proximate cause) and why it evolved (ultimate cause).
points: Innate behavior (instinct, no learning needed): reflex action, fixed action pattern (a set sequence that runs to completion once triggered), kinesis (random movement that speeds up or slows in response to a stimulus), taxis (directed movement toward or away from something, like phototaxis toward light), migration (seasonal long-distance moves, triggered by day length).
Communication uses a signal: chemical (pheromones), visual (displays), sound (alarm calls), touch. Displays include the courtship display, aggressive display and distraction display.

Groups: foraging for food, altruism, and kin selection (helping relatives pass on shared genes). Mating systems: monogamy (one pair), polygyny (one male, many females), polyandry (one female, many males). Sexual selection: intrasexual selection (same sex competing) and intersexual selection (mate choice).
Learned behavior: habituation (learning to ignore a harmless stimulus), imprinting (early bonding, like ducklings following their mother).
Conditioned behavior: classical conditioning (Pavlov's dog links a bell with food), operant conditioning (a behavior linked to a reward or punishment).
Cognitive learning: problem solving and reasoning (rats learning mazes, chimps stacking boxes). Sociobiology explains social behavior through evolution.

7.why: Salmon make thousands of eggs and most die young: Type III.

38.why: In every symbiosis, at least one species benefits.

39.why: Pioneer species colonize bare ground and start succession.

40.why: Secondary succession: groups of species replace each other in stages.

42.why: Innate = automatic responses. Learned = changes with experience.

43.why: Phototaxis = moving toward or away from light.

44.why: Butterflies that migrated survived and reproduced, so natural selection favored migration.

47.why: Helping relatives pass on shared genes = kin selection.

48.why: Male cardinals fighting rivals for territory spend energy to win mates.

50.why: One devoted male helps raise healthier offspring.

51.why: Cognitive learning is the most complex type, using many brain processes.

52.why: Operant: a voluntary behavior linked to its consequences. Classical: an involuntary response linked to a new stimulus.

53.why: Use mark and recapture to estimate size, then density = size ÷ area.

54.why: Same range and same number = same density, but one herds (clumped) and one is random.

55.why: Many young but few adults → high death rate before maturity. Test it with a life table.

56.why: Few offspring means losing even one is a big risk.

57.why: Sterile workers put their energy into the hive and raising the queen's offspring (their relatives).

58.why: Many seeds: most energy goes into numbers, and few survive. Few seeds: energy goes into making each one likely to survive.

59.why: Fleas reproduce much faster (higher rmax), so you study them over a shorter time.

60.why: N roughly doubles every month (exponential). It'll level off (logistic) when resources run short.

61.why: Warming helps drought-resistant plants and hurts others.

62.why: Density-independent (pesticide) kills regardless of numbers. Density-dependent (running out of food) bites harder when crowded.

63.why: Frogs spend their energy making huge numbers of eggs, leaving little for care.

64.why: The curve is still rising steeply (exponentially), so it would likely keep growing.

65.why: The base is only slightly wider than the middle: slow growth.

66.why: Machines boosted farming, which raised resources (K) and allowed exponential growth.

67.why: A fairly even spread across ages suggests a developed country.

68.why: We passed 1.0 Earth around 1987. Our demand for land and resources exceeds what Earth supplies. If it keeps rising, our population could crash.

69.why: Real data include every influence (weather, disease, food), not just predator-prey effects.

70.why: What's measured, wolves and elk, are the dependent variables.

71.why: They feed in different places, so they don't directly compete and can coexist.

72.why: Bees get nectar and plants get pollinated: mutualism.

75.why: Those with the response survived and passed it on.

76.why: The threatened fish released chemical alarm signals that flowed to the other tank.

77.why: Brighter males had more surviving chicks, so brightness signals fitness.

78.why: Females holding rich territories attract several males: polyandry.

79.why: Bell + food → eventually the bell alone causes drooling.

84.why: Shade = less light = less photosynthesis, so less energy for everyone.

85.why: Uniform spacing often comes from plants releasing chemicals that block neighbors.

86.why: Flies that stored energy instead of breeding early survived cold better, so selection favored that trade-off.

87.why: Without food, females lived shorter lives and laid fewer eggs, putting energy toward survival over reproduction.

95.why: Waste grows with the population, and dealing with it eats into habitats.
